title_original: Reflections from Damaged Life: After the Hunt
editorial_excerpt_zh: 课程取消：在卢卡·瓜达尼诺的《猎场》中，文件夹是空的，是因为教授们满口胡言，还是仅仅是一个穿帮镜头？
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的注意力本该放在别处。在一个坦都里餐厅的场景中，哲学教授汉克（安德鲁·加菲尔德饰）向他的系同事兼朋友阿尔玛（朱莉娅·罗伯茨饰）吐露了针对他的性侵指控，我却忍不住盯着汉克敞开的信使包。具体来说，是包里面那个空的、三孔的蓝色文件夹，尺寸大概是1.5”或者2”。汉克情绪激昂、充满防御性，声音也太大。阿尔玛仔细地看着他。她没有吃东西。但为什么文件夹里什么都没有呢？我不禁纳闷。这就是他带去上课的东西吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我琢磨着，这个文件夹倒是挺适合汉克的。他空洞而傲慢，是耶鲁大学这个精英世界里那种人们熟知的年轻教授典型（穿着牛仔裤，露出一丛胸毛），至少在卢卡·瓜达尼诺于《猎场》中所构想的耶鲁是如此。瓜达尼诺的耶鲁与克里斯托弗·鲁福和其他右翼十字军所抨击的那版精英大学有很多共同点。它富有、势利且令人难以忍受，尽管其左翼自由主义政治立场已经被调得非常低。别误会我。这一切是否类似于“真实的耶鲁”并不重要——尽管这部电影大部分是在英国拍摄的，由剑桥大学充当纽黑文那所大学的哥特式外观。但你也不应把这部电影误认为是一部带有现实世界关切的严肃剧情片。在超越“耶鲁情绪板”的阶段之前，《猎场》似乎并没有得到多少深入开发。陈设或许很考究，但角色及其冲突却并非如此。简而言之，它是它试图描绘的地方的一种幻想，而且是个轻飘飘的幻想。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "坐在权力金字塔顶端的是阿尔玛，她堪称某种女王，受到身边所有人的仰慕。自然地，她唯一能走的路就是下坡。她的明星研究生玛吉（阿yo·埃德贝里饰）崇拜她，可能也渴望得到她。汉克公开调情，而阿尔玛的心理分析师丈夫弗雷德里克（一如既往精彩的迈克尔·斯特图巴饰）则忍受这一切，而且大多表现得优雅。在阿尔玛和弗雷德里克那震惊般巨大而奢华的公寓举办派对后，汉克步行送玛吉回家，正如玛吉后来在楼梯间声泪俱下的忏悔中所向阿尔玛倾诉的那样，他对她实施了性侵。至少她是这么告诉她的导师的，而导师的反应却缺乏同情。与此同时，汉克愤愤不平地坚称自己是无辜的。阿尔玛此前一直享受着汉克和玛吉的奉承，此刻几乎感到被冒犯，仿佛他们两个怎么会转而向她寻求帮助。一场关于取消文化、#MeToo、种族和特权的意料之中的危机落入了她的怀抱，直到它也将她吞没。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "要让美国的甜心变成一个冷若冰霜的碧池并不容易——而阿尔玛用了更严厉的词来形容自己。罗伯茨轻而易举地做到了。她那标志性的灿烂笑容变成了一个紧抿嘴唇的苦笑；她那栗色的蓬松头发如今变成了带有深色发根的金发，经过两次染发并精心梳理。尽管整个演员阵容都奉献了杰出的表演，包括几乎让人认不出来的科洛·塞维尼——她顶着一头蓬乱的“英勇王子”齐耳短发，饰演大学心理医生——但罗伯茨依然是焦点。她几乎在电影的每一秒都出现在银幕上，给我们充足的时间去端详她那张坚硬、瓷器般的脸，这张脸除了冷漠、恼怒，以及随着电影进展而显露出的赤裸裸的蔑视之外，什么也没有给我们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "瓜达尼诺对教授们所做的工作基本不感兴趣，因此电影中的所有知识分子引文都显得毫无意义。片中充满了各种名号的抛售，但其目的是为了营造一种精致感，或许还有丑角般的滑稽。“亚里士多德是个仇外者！”“弗洛伊德是个厌女症者！”——这些既不好笑也不深刻的俏皮话，就是阿尔玛圈子里所谓的闲聊。我发现有一个场景格外令人不快：阿尔玛试图在一个研究生研讨班上讲授西奥多·阿多诺的《最低限度的道德》：此时的阿尔玛显然已经精神崩溃，她正严厉训斥一个名叫凯蒂（塔迪亚·格雷厄姆饰）的亚裔学生。“霸凌”或许是更贴切的词。在此之前，凯蒂一言未发，但她勇敢地对文本做出了诠释，提到了汉娜·阿伦特对《奥德赛》的解读，特别是英雄奥德修斯在听到别人歌唱他的事迹时开始对自己有所了解的那一刻。阿尔玛抛出了一些关于“他者”的术语黑话。凯蒂退回了沉默。她知道自己触动了某根神经。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿尔玛不想从外部审视自己；她只在内部感到舒适，最好是在哲学部门的狭小天地之内。“狭隘”这个词根本不足以形容它。在某些特写镜头中，摄影师马利克·哈桑·赛义德的相机的景深是如此之浅，以至于半张脸都对不准焦。外部世界几乎触及不到阿尔玛的世界。“难道你没有一些晦涩的抗议要去公开愤怒吗？”她冲着玛吉的伴侣啐道，而且她还不断用错后者的性别代词。有一段时间，我还以为这是一部时代剧，带着伍迪·艾伦风格的片名字体和卷起袖子的巨大西装外套（就像罗伯茨和阿曼达·塞弗里德今年在威尼斯电影节上穿的同款服装）。然后我看到了一部手机。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "既然这是一部瓜达尼诺的电影，你或许会好奇阿尔玛在过着怎样的性生活。答案显然是：没有。除了权力，她唯一渴望的似乎就是堆在办公桌上的垃圾食品（感谢Bonchon炸鸡盒的赞助）。当阿尔玛发现弗雷德里克正对着网络色情片打鼾、身旁还散落着几团揉皱的纸巾时，片中开了一个低级玩笑——但至少人家还发泄出来了！如果所有的主要角色都是男性，这部电影似乎不太可能会变得如此毫无性欲。“[我非常了解的一件事]是男人之间的爱，”瓜达尼诺曾在接受《Fantastic Man》杂志采访时说，“另一件事是两个男人之间任何关系背后都存在的底层情欲，无论他们是同性恋还是异性恋。在合适的条件下，任何直男都能与另一个男人建立起不离不弃的纽带，甚至可能比和女人之间还要深厚。”也许对这位导演来说，问题在于他根本无法想象女性究竟该如何与任何人建立起“不离不弃的纽带”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "无论多么虚弱无能，《猎场之后》中的男性角色们依然比他们身边那些野心勃勃的女性过着更丰富的生活。（阿尔玛甚至在一处情节中去听了一场题为“圣战主义的未来是女性”的讲座，我真拿不准这究竟是不是在讽刺。）弗雷德里克听迈尔斯·戴维斯、现代主义音乐和雷鬼，还会做一道精美的卡苏莱砂锅菜，而阿尔玛却对之冷嘲热讽。就连汉克，在情绪大发雷霆的间隙也不忘抽出时间背两句莎士比亚。与此同时，在阿尔玛的床头柜上，放着一本倒扣着的托马斯·曼的小说《布登勃洛克一家》以及几粒药丸。她伸手去拿那些药丸。而打扮得和阿尔玛一模一样的玛吉，对导师的研究甚至超过了对阿甘本（她据称在论文中抄袭了这位学者的观点）的研究。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿尔玛是个很难让人喜欢的角色，但你又根本无法将目光从她身上移开。她就像是一座宏伟跳蚤马戏团里那根漂亮的帐篷支柱。也许这就是汉克轻描淡写地提到“高等教育危机”时的真正含义：指的并不是针对平权法案（affirmative action）和多元、平权与包容（DEI）的那些非常真实的文化战争，也不是为了更具实用性和可剥削性的STEM学科而对人文探索进行的肢解——而是像托马斯·曼的《威尼斯之死》中那样，一个处于高度衰退状态的旧秩序。也许正因如此，阿尔玛的指甲才被涂成光泽的黑色，以此暗示腐朽。不过它们看起来确实也很美。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "瓜达尼诺对曼那种矛盾心理毫无兴趣。他喜欢沉溺于这个令人窒息的世界里，沉溺于其中丰富的红酒和缀有流苏的靠枕。人文学院院长在片中最生硬的一句台词中坦言：“我发现自己做的是视觉效果的生意，而不是实质内容。”这番言论的空洞究竟是体制的过错还是电影拍摄的问题，目前尚不清楚。换作另一部电影，或许会去探讨那种对耶鲁这类地方的讽刺性看法——而在我看来这种看法完全合情合理，即丑闻永远无法真正动摇这所大学，违规者只会受到轻惩甚至一路平步青云，而权力结构最终分毫未损。但如果瓜达尼诺真的试图进行批判，那么如果他的电影不是把常春藤盟校（或者说任何美国大学）的真实面貌拍得如此草率，其批判力度本可以更强。我只有一些微不足道的挑剔，比如奇怪地不见了踪影的花呢面料，或者像阿尔玛这样备受尊崇的教授为何至今仍未获得终身教职（tenure）的疑问。但说真的，这一切里面职权法案第九条办公室（Title IX office）究竟在哪？耶鲁大学本身又在哪里？它那些不那么秘密的秘密社团在哪里？那些源源不断产出的美国总统、最高法院大法官以及在很大程度上统治着世界的人物又都在哪里？是因为教授们满嘴谎言才导致文件夹空空如也，还是这纯粹只是一个穿帮失误？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "瓜达尼诺曾表达过改编《布登勃洛克一家》的兴趣，我也非常欢迎这位不安分、胃口极杂的导演给出他的诠释。不过，我只希望他能放过原著中的角色，别让他们落得像阿尔玛那样的下场。曼这部小说的真正伟大之处之一，在于其中有一个场景：一个角色在阅读哲学时被唤醒了生机——确切地说，是叔本华。在好几页的篇幅里，世界对他的而言宛如新生。他深受触动。随后，他才渐渐重新沉沦回自己以前那种缓慢而沉闷的生活中去。要是阿尔玛也能被某种思想所触动，哪怕只是一点来自外界的、意想不到的东西，那该有多好啊。哪怕只有短短一瞬间，或许也足以去正视并抚平所有的痛苦。", "translated": true}]

Specifically, at the empty three-ring binder inside the bag, blue, either 1.5” or 2”. Hank is animated, defensive, and too loud. Alma watches him carefully. She does not eat. But why isn’t there anything in the binder? I kept wondering. Is that what he is bringing to teach?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The binder, I decided, suits Hank quite well. He is empty and arrogant, a recognizable type of younger professor (in jeans and with an exposed tuft of chest hair) within the rarified world of Yale, at least as Luca Guadagnino imagines it in After the Hunt . And Guadagnino’s Yale has a lot in common with the version of elite universities Christopher Rufo and other right-wing crusaders have railed against. It is rich, elitist, and insufferable, even if its left-liberal politics are dialed very far down. Don’t get me wrong. Whether any of this resembles the “real Yale” is unimportant—though most of the film was shot in England, with Cambridge standing in for the New Haven university’s gothic exteriors. But neither should you mistake the film for a serious drama with real-world concerns. After the Hunt doesn’t seem to have been developed very far past the “Yale mood board” stage. The furnishings may be elaborate, but the characters and their conflicts are less so. It is, in short, a fantasy of the place it attempts to depict, and a flimsy one at that."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Atop this world sits Alma, who is something of a queen, admired by everyone around her. Naturally, the only direction for her to go is down. Her star graduate student, Maggie (Ayo Edebiri), worships her and possibly desires her as well. Hank is openly flirtatious, and Alma’s psychoanalyst husband Frederik (the always-wonderful Michael Stuhlbarg) puts up with all this, mostly gracefully. After a party at Alma and Frederik’s shockingly large and opulent apartment, Hank walks Maggie home, and, as Maggie later recounts to Alma in a tearful stairwell confession, he sexually assaults her. At least this is what she tells her mentor, whose reaction is less than sympathetic. Meanwhile, Hank indignantly maintains his innocence. Alma, who has so far enjoyed both Hank and Maggie’s flattery, seems almost offended that either of them would turn to her for help. A predictable crisis of cancel culture, #MeToo, race, and privilege spills into her lap, until it engulfs her too."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It takes a lot to turn America’s sweetheart into a frosty bitch—and Alma uses an even harsher word to describe herself. Roberts manages it handily. Her wide smile is transformed into a tight-lipped grimace; her auburn mane, now blonde with dark roots, is twice-dyed and carefully coiffed. Though the entire cast gives outstanding performances, including a nearly unrecognizable Chloë Sevigny in a shaggy Prince Valiant bob as the university psychiatrist, Roberts is the focus. She is on screen for nearly every second of the film, giving us ample time to study her hard, porcelain face, which gives us nothing but diffidence, irritation, and, as the film goes on, raw contempt."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Guadagnino is mostly uninterested in the work that professors do, so none of the film’s intellectual references make much sense. There is plenty of name-dropping, but it’s meant to conjure an air of sophistication, and perhaps buffoonery. “Aristotle was a xenophobe!” “Freud was a misogynist!”—these one-liners, neither funny nor insightful, are what count for banter in Alma’s circle. I found a scene in which Alma tries to teach Theodor Adorno’s Minima Moralia in a graduate seminar especially unpleasant: Alma, by now clearly unraveling, upbraids an Asian student named Katie (Thaddea Graham). “Bullies” is the better word. Until this point, Katie has not said a word, but she braves an interpretation of the text, pointing to Hannah Arendt’s reading of The Odyssey , particularly a moment in which the hero Odysseus comes to understand something about himself when he hears someone else singing about his endeavors. Alma unleashes some jargony nonsense about “the Other.” Katie falls back into silence. She knows she’s touched a nerve."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alma does not want to see herself from the outside; she is comfortable only within, and ideally within the confines of the philosophy department. Insularity hardly begins to describe it. In certain close-up shots, the depth of field of cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed’s camera is so shallow that half of a face appears out of focus. The outside world scarcely touches Alma’s. “Don’t you have some obscure protest to be publicly angry at?” she spits at Maggie’s partner, whom she also continually misgenders. For a while I thought this might be a period film, with the Woody Allen–style title cards and the giant blazers rolled up at the sleeves (like the identical outfits that Roberts and Amanda Seyfried wore at this year’s Venice Film Festival). Then I saw a cell phone."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This being a Guadagnino film, you might be wondering what kind of sex Alma is having. The answer is none, apparently. The only thing she seems to desire, other than power, is the junk food that she eats at her desk (props to the box of Bonchon). There’s a cheap joke when Alma finds Frederik snoring to internet porn and a couple of crumpled tissues, but at least he got off! If all the lead characters had been male, it seems unlikely the film would have remained so sexless. “One [thing I’m very knowledgeable about] is the love between men,” Guadagnino once said in an interview with Fantastic Man Magazine, “and the other is the erotic tension that’s underlying any relationship between two men, gay or straight. Given the right circumstances, any straight man can bond relentlessly with another man, and maybe even more deeply than with a woman.” Maybe the problem, for him, is imagining how women can “bond relentlessly” with anyone at all."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "However weak and castrated, the men in After the Hunt lead richer lives than the hyper-ambitious women around them. (At one point Alma attends a lecture titled “The Future of Jihadism is Female,” which I’m not sure is meant to be taken as satire.) Frederik listens to Miles Davis, modernist music, and reggae, and he cooks a beautiful cassoulet, which Alma mocks. Even Hank, in the middle of a tantrum, spares a moment to spout Shakespeare. Meanwhile, on Alma’s bedside table lies an overturned copy of Thomas Mann’s Buddenbrooks and a couple of pills. She reaches for the pills. And Maggie, dressed like Alma, studies her mentor more closely than her Agamben (whom she allegedly plagiarized for her dissertation)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alma is a difficult character to like, but she’s impossible not to watch. She is like a beautiful tentpole for a decadent flea circus. Maybe this is what Hank means when he refers glibly to a “crisis in higher education”: not the very real culture war against affirmative action and DEI, or the dismantling of humanistic inquiry in favor of STEM fields seen as more practical and exploitable—but, like in Mann’s Death in Venice , an old order in an advanced state of decline. Perhaps this is why Alma’s nails are painted a glossy black, to suggest rot. But they also look great."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Guadagnino has little of Mann’s ambivalence. He enjoys luxuriating in this airless world, with its bountiful red wine and tasseled pillows. The dean of humanities admits as much in one of the movie’s clunkiest lines: “I found myself in the business of optics, not substance.” It’s unclear if the vapidity of such a statement is a fault of the institution or the filmmaking. Another movie might have entertained the cynical—and to my mind entirely justifiable—view of places like Yale where scandals never really rock the university, offenders receive light penalties or even fail upward, and the structure of power remains ultimately unchanged. But if Guadagnino is attempting critique, it would land harder if his film were not such a sloppy depiction of what an Ivy League (or really any American) university is actually like. I have small quibbles, like the curious absence of tweed, or the question of why such an esteemed professor like Alma has not yet secured tenure. But seriously, where is the Title IX office in all of this? Or Yale itself, with its not-so-secret societies and its steady stream of U.S. presidents, Supreme Court justices, and people who in no small part run the world? Are the binders empty because the professors are full of shit, or is it just a continuity error?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Guadagnino has expressed an interest in adapting Buddenbrooks , and I would welcome an interpretation from this restless, omnivorous director. I only hope, however, that he spares its characters the fate he gives to Alma. One of the things that makes Mann’s novel truly great is a scene in which a character comes alive reading philosophy—Schopenhauer, to be precise. For several pages, the world seems new to him. He is profoundly moved. Then he gradually sinks back into the slow, dull life he had been living before. If only Alma, too, could be excited by an idea, something from the outside, unexpected. Even for a moment, that might be enough to justify all the misery."}]
article_text:
My attention should have been elsewhere. During a scene in a tandoori restaurant in which philosophy professor Hank (Andrew Garfield) confides in his department colleague and friend Alma (Julia Roberts) about sexual assault allegations that have been made against him, I couldn’t help but stare at Hank’s open messenger bag. Specifically, at the empty three-ring binder inside the bag, blue, either 1.5” or 2”. Hank is animated, defensive, and too loud. Alma watches him carefully. She does not eat. But why isn’t there anything in the binder? I kept wondering. Is that what he is bringing to teach?

The binder, I decided, suits Hank quite well. He is empty and arrogant, a recognizable type of younger professor (in jeans and with an exposed tuft of chest hair) within the rarified world of Yale, at least as Luca Guadagnino imagines it in After the Hunt . And Guadagnino’s Yale has a lot in common with the version of elite universities Christopher Rufo and other right-wing crusaders have railed against. It is rich, elitist, and insufferable, even if its left-liberal politics are dialed very far down. Don’t get me wrong. Whether any of this resembles the “real Yale” is unimportant—though most of the film was shot in England, with Cambridge standing in for the New Haven university’s gothic exteriors. But neither should you mistake the film for a serious drama with real-world concerns. After the Hunt doesn’t seem to have been developed very far past the “Yale mood board” stage. The furnishings may be elaborate, but the characters and their conflicts are less so. It is, in short, a fantasy of the place it attempts to depict, and a flimsy one at that.

Atop this world sits Alma, who is something of a queen, admired by everyone around her. Naturally, the only direction for her to go is down. Her star graduate student, Maggie (Ayo Edebiri), worships her and possibly desires her as well. Hank is openly flirtatious, and Alma’s psychoanalyst husband Frederik (the always-wonderful Michael Stuhlbarg) puts up with all this, mostly gracefully. After a party at Alma and Frederik’s shockingly large and opulent apartment, Hank walks Maggie home, and, as Maggie later recounts to Alma in a tearful stairwell confession, he sexually assaults her. At least this is what she tells her mentor, whose reaction is less than sympathetic. Meanwhile, Hank indignantly maintains his innocence. Alma, who has so far enjoyed both Hank and Maggie’s flattery, seems almost offended that either of them would turn to her for help. A predictable crisis of cancel culture, #MeToo, race, and privilege spills into her lap, until it engulfs her too.

It takes a lot to turn America’s sweetheart into a frosty bitch—and Alma uses an even harsher word to describe herself. Roberts manages it handily. Her wide smile is transformed into a tight-lipped grimace; her auburn mane, now blonde with dark roots, is twice-dyed and carefully coiffed. Though the entire cast gives outstanding performances, including a nearly unrecognizable Chloë Sevigny in a shaggy Prince Valiant bob as the university psychiatrist, Roberts is the focus. She is on screen for nearly every second of the film, giving us ample time to study her hard, porcelain face, which gives us nothing but diffidence, irritation, and, as the film goes on, raw contempt.

Guadagnino is mostly uninterested in the work that professors do, so none of the film’s intellectual references make much sense. There is plenty of name-dropping, but it’s meant to conjure an air of sophistication, and perhaps buffoonery. “Aristotle was a xenophobe!” “Freud was a misogynist!”—these one-liners, neither funny nor insightful, are what count for banter in Alma’s circle. I found a scene in which Alma tries to teach Theodor Adorno’s Minima Moralia in a graduate seminar especially unpleasant: Alma, by now clearly unraveling, upbraids an Asian student named Katie (Thaddea Graham). “Bullies” is the better word. Until this point, Katie has not said a word, but she braves an interpretation of the text, pointing to Hannah Arendt’s reading of The Odyssey , particularly a moment in which the hero Odysseus comes to understand something about himself when he hears someone else singing about his endeavors. Alma unleashes some jargony nonsense about “the Other.” Katie falls back into silence. She knows she’s touched a nerve.

Alma does not want to see herself from the outside; she is comfortable only within, and ideally within the confines of the philosophy department. Insularity hardly begins to describe it. In certain close-up shots, the depth of field of cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed’s camera is so shallow that half of a face appears out of focus. The outside world scarcely touches Alma’s. “Don’t you have some obscure protest to be publicly angry at?” she spits at Maggie’s partner, whom she also continually misgenders. For a while I thought this might be a period film, with the Woody Allen–style title cards and the giant blazers rolled up at the sleeves (like the identical outfits that Roberts and Amanda Seyfried wore at this year’s Venice Film Festival). Then I saw a cell phone.

This being a Guadagnino film, you might be wondering what kind of sex Alma is having. The answer is none, apparently. The only thing she seems to desire, other than power, is the junk food that she eats at her desk (props to the box of Bonchon). There’s a cheap joke when Alma finds Frederik snoring to internet porn and a couple of crumpled tissues, but at least he got off! If all the lead characters had been male, it seems unlikely the film would have remained so sexless. “One [thing I’m very knowledgeable about] is the love between men,” Guadagnino once said in an interview with Fantastic Man Magazine, “and the other is the erotic tension that’s underlying any relationship between two men, gay or straight. Given the right circumstances, any straight man can bond relentlessly with another man, and maybe even more deeply than with a woman.” Maybe the problem, for him, is imagining how women can “bond relentlessly” with anyone at all.

However weak and castrated, the men in After the Hunt lead richer lives than the hyper-ambitious women around them. (At one point Alma attends a lecture titled “The Future of Jihadism is Female,” which I’m not sure is meant to be taken as satire.) Frederik listens to Miles Davis, modernist music, and reggae, and he cooks a beautiful cassoulet, which Alma mocks. Even Hank, in the middle of a tantrum, spares a moment to spout Shakespeare. Meanwhile, on Alma’s bedside table lies an overturned copy of Thomas Mann’s Buddenbrooks and a couple of pills. She reaches for the pills. And Maggie, dressed like Alma, studies her mentor more closely than her Agamben (whom she allegedly plagiarized for her dissertation).

Alma is a difficult character to like, but she’s impossible not to watch. She is like a beautiful tentpole for a decadent flea circus. Maybe this is what Hank means when he refers glibly to a “crisis in higher education”: not the very real culture war against affirmative action and DEI, or the dismantling of humanistic inquiry in favor of STEM fields seen as more practical and exploitable—but, like in Mann’s Death in Venice , an old order in an advanced state of decline. Perhaps this is why Alma’s nails are painted a glossy black, to suggest rot. But they also look great.

Guadagnino has little of Mann’s ambivalence. He enjoys luxuriating in this airless world, with its bountiful red wine and tasseled pillows. The dean of humanities admits as much in one of the movie’s clunkiest lines: “I found myself in the business of optics, not substance.” It’s unclear if the vapidity of such a statement is a fault of the institution or the filmmaking. Another movie might have entertained the cynical—and to my mind entirely justifiable—view of places like Yale where scandals never really rock the university, offenders receive light penalties or even fail upward, and the structure of power remains ultimately unchanged. But if Guadagnino is attempting critique, it would land harder if his film were not such a sloppy depiction of what an Ivy League (or really any American) university is actually like. I have small quibbles, like the curious absence of tweed, or the question of why such an esteemed professor like Alma has not yet secured tenure. But seriously, where is the Title IX office in all of this? Or Yale itself, with its not-so-secret societies and its steady stream of U.S. presidents, Supreme Court justices, and people who in no small part run the world? Are the binders empty because the professors are full of shit, or is it just a continuity error?

Guadagnino has expressed an interest in adapting Buddenbrooks , and I would welcome an interpretation from this restless, omnivorous director. I only hope, however, that he spares its characters the fate he gives to Alma. One of the things that makes Mann’s novel truly great is a scene in which a character comes alive reading philosophy—Schopenhauer, to be precise. For several pages, the world seems new to him. He is profoundly moved. Then he gradually sinks back into the slow, dull life he had been living before. If only Alma, too, could be excited by an idea, something from the outside, unexpected. Even for a moment, that might be enough to justify all the misery.
excerpt_original: Class canceled: are the binders empty in Luca Guadagnino’s After the Hunt because the professors are full of shit, or is it just a continuity error?

title_original: Muralnomad: Batima Zaurbekova’s “Threads of Heritage”

"哈萨克斯坦著名的纺织品传统长期以来一直反映着这个中亚草原国家作为贸易帝国、迁徙路线和文化传播交汇点的历史身份。世界上已知最古老的古手工打结绒毛地毯是巴澤雷克（Pazyryk）地毯，可追溯至公元前5世纪；它是在巴泽雷克文化的皇家墓穴中被发现的，这是一种铁器时代的游牧文化，曾在现今西伯利亚、哈萨克斯坦、蒙古和中国境内的阿尔泰山脉地区繁荣发展。壁毯和壁挂是中亚游牧建筑中的传统陈设，用勒·柯布西耶的话说，这些“羊毛墙”将圆顶帐篷（yurts）变成了家。沙皇俄国和苏联的发展催生了阿拉木图第一所壁毯学校——地毯艺术合作社（Kovroschitsa "作为1960年代和70年代哈萨克斯坦蓬勃发展的壁毯艺术流派中的首位女性艺术家，考虑到在苏联宪法保障妇女平权的背景下依然存在的父权制规范，扎乌尔别科娃的成就更显弥足珍贵。她于1946年出生于哈萨克苏维埃社会主义共和国江布尔州富尔曼诺夫卡村的一个工匠家庭；她的母亲是地毯工匠，叔叔是珠宝匠。童年时期的扎乌尔别科娃酷爱音乐，但最终选择学习绘画，因为她的母亲认为这是一个更为体面的职业。她于1969年毕业于阿拉木图艺术学校，后来又在阿拜哈萨克国立师范大学获得了应用艺术专业学位。", "现实中的扎乌尔别科娃充满活力且直言不讳。她坦言，法国对她作为艺术家的影响最深。“1982年我去了罗马、佛罗伦萨、威尼斯进行了一次巡游……到处都是露天博物馆。我去法国办过一次展览，我必须承认我取得了巨大成功；他们甚至邀请我留下来。但那是苏联时期，我必须回到我的祖国……我在各处都能找到灵感。你看得越多，你的作品就会变得越成熟。”她回忆起自己曾参加每一个受邀的展览，每天工作16到18个小时以赶上截止日期。她分别于1989年和1991年在巴黎、1995年在阿拉木图、1998年在米兰、1999年在卢加诺举办了她的首批展览。从1997年到2000年，她生活在土耳其——一个她感到极具亲和力的国家，在此期间她在安卡拉、伊斯坦布尔和其他土耳其城市举办了9场展览。", Taeuber-Arp）相近，并未做过多展开。与传统壁毯的色调和设计相比，扎乌尔别科娃在《在蒙古包里》（1985）等作品中对具象与抽象的实验具有明显的表现力和大胆风格。即使在这些早期范例中，她看似无拘无束的设计也类似于随性自由的绘画，而她明亮、复杂的色彩组合和过渡则以精湛的技术和自信为基础。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "在1970年代，哈萨克斯坦经历了快速的工业化与城市化，与此同时也伴随着一系列紧迫的危机：咸海的干涸、位于东北部的塞米巴拉金斯克持续进行的苏联核试验，以及赫鲁晓夫灾难性的垦荒运动所造成的严重环境退化。面对这种不可逆转甚至关乎存亡的变革，在展览第二部分中，扎乌尔别科娃的巨幅壁毯背后支撑着一种对生态、社会和文化和谐的堂吉诃德式追求。《辽阔》（1975）、《哈萨克斯坦》（1977）和《大地母亲》（1984）等大型作品最为引人注目的是其半抽象构图，它们将人类形体、山脉、树木和水流融为一体；风、空气和光线也被赋予了色彩、形状和实体感。《大地母亲》被扎乌尔别科娃誉为她技术要求最高的一个项目，充分展现了艺术家将土地、农业和女性主题融为一体的波浪状涡卷技巧。展览的核心作品《辽阔》呈现了一个宏伟的前失乐园式的世界，它以一座风格化的蒙古包和女性形象为核心，周围环绕着音乐家、动植物散发出的光芒四射的波纹。其万花筒般的色彩渐变极为错综复杂且精准，甚至将极小人物的颧骨都刻画得亲切细腻，同时在宏大的色彩交响中统一了各种不同的风景元素。扎乌尔别科娃估计，这幅长207厘米、宽361厘米的壁毯耗时大约6个月制作完成；她指出，挑选线团的颜色往往是整个过程中最具挑战性的部分，尤其是在描绘色彩渐变极细微的平面时。", "扎乌尔别科娃在1970年代末和80年代的集约创作期与其日益提升的专业认可相得益彰。1977年，国家委托她与其他三位艺术家为哈萨克斯坦酒店制作了一幅100平方米的壁毯。这件具有地标意义的作品名为《彩虹》，耗时两年制作完成，并被收入哈萨克斯坦电影制片厂于1977年出品的关于扎乌尔别科娃的纪录片《旋律》中。苏联解体和1991年哈萨克斯坦独立后，扎乌尔别科娃前往土耳其，以期从这些转型期带来的精疲力竭中获得喘息。紧随苏联解体之后的时期对于哈萨克斯坦艺术家而言充满艰难，因为文化部停止了艺术品委托创作。然而，不断拓展的国际交往机遇促进了更深层次的文化交流，也激发了公众对艺术日益增长的兴趣。1997年，索罗斯基金会在阿拉木图开设了索罗斯当代艺术中心；尽管因其暗含新自由主义议程而饱受批评，但在其运营10年后关闭之前，它一直是独立艺术家的重要平台。", article_text:
Shows

Muralnomad: Batima Zaurbekova’s “Threads of Heritage”

BATIMA ZAURBEKOVA ,

Gifts of the Sea , 2004, tapestry, wool, weaving, 83 x 119 cm. Copyright and courtesy the artist.

Batima Zaurbekova Threads of Heritage Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts Almaty Sep 25–Nov 8, 2026

In 1952, Le Corbusier declared tapestry “the ‘mural’ of modern times,” the perfect complement for the internationally mobile nomad in an era of revolutionary speed, time, and motion. His term “muralnomads” not only refers to the textiles’ portable nature but also serves as, in scholar Daisy King’s words, “a metaphor for the nomadic inheritance of their making, that in turn mirrors the migration, displacement, and complexity of modernism itself.” “Threads of Heritage,” the solo exhibition by the octogenarian Kazakhstani artist Batima Zaurbekova featuring over 80 tapestries, paintings, and sketches, offers a unique opportunity to consider her works not only within historical lineages but also as personal expressions of postcolonial utopianism, mobility, and progressiveness.

Kazakhstan’s celebrated textile heritage has long mirrored the Central Asian steppe nation’s historic identity as a locus of trading empires, migratory routes, and cultural transmission. The world’s oldest known hand-knotted pile carpet is the Pazyryk rug dating to the fifth century B.C.; it was discovered in a royal tomb of the Pazyryks, a nomadic Iron Age culture that flourished in the Altai Mountain region within present-day Siberia, Kazakhstan, Mongolia, and China. Tapestries and wall hangings are traditional fixtures in Central Asian nomadic architecture where the “woolen walls,” to use Le Corbusier’s term, transformed yurts into homes. Imperial Russian and Soviet developments gave rise to Almaty’s first tapestry school, the Kovroschitsa Artel, which was founded by the artist Nikolai Tsivchinskiy. Tsivchinskiy was born in Saint Petersburg in 1905, studied and worked in Ukraine producing tapestries at the Kyiv Experimental School, and moved to Almaty in 1937 to escape Stalin’s repression. Another important founder of Kazakh tapestries is Kurasbek Tynybekov, who was born in 1947 and studied in Ukraine; he taught at the Almaty Art College in the early 1970s, where he mentored the young Zaurbekova.

BATIMA ZAURBEKOVA ’s “Threads of Heritage” at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts, Almaty, 2026. Photo by Kirill Fedorov. Courtesy the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts.

As the first female artist in Kazakhstan’s burgeoning school of tapestry art in the 1960s and ’70s, Zaurbekova is all the more estimable for her achievement considering the patriarchal norms that persisted despite women’s equality under the Soviet constitution. She was born in 1946 in the village of Furmanovka in the Zhambul region of the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic to an artisanal family; her mother was a carpet artisan and her uncle a jeweler. As a child, Zaurbekova loved music but chose to study painting, which her mother considered a more reputable profession. She graduated from the Alma-Ata Art School in 1969 and later obtained a specialization in applied arts from the Abai Kazakh National Pedagogical University.

In person, Zaurbekova is vivacious and outspoken. She confesses that France had the greatest influence on her as an artist. “In 1982 I had a tour of Rome, Florence, Venice… Everywhere it was an open-air museum. I went to France for an exhibition, and I must admit I was very successful; they even asked me to stay. But those were Soviet times and I had to return to my country… I found inspiration everywhere. The more you see, the more sophisticated your work becomes.” She recalls participating in every exhibition she was invited to, working 16 to 18 hours a day to meet deadlines. She held her first exhibitions in Paris in 1989 and 1991, in Almaty in 1995, Milan in 1998 and Lugano in 1999. From 1997 to 2000 she lived in Turkey, a country for which she felt a great affinity, and held nine exhibitions in Ankara, Istanbul, and other Turkish cities during this period.

BATIMA ZAURBEKOVA , Waiting , 1980, gouache on paper, 35 x 41 cm (left); and Sketch for the Family tapestry , 2017, oil on canvas (right). Copyright and courtesy the artist.

The exhibition’s Russian curator Alina Fedorovich has made a remarkable effort to position Zaurbekova’s work within the pantheon of Western modernist artists and thinkers, including Claude Lévi-Strauss’s logic of mythological art and Sonia Delaunay’s geometric abstractions. A missed opportunity is the relative lack of explication of Kazakh cultural motifs, as well as the cultural milieu of Zaurbekova’s contemporaries. For example, the first section shows a selection of Zaurbekova’s early works, installed on freestanding temporary walls surrounded by the museum’s permanent displays of ornamental furniture, tapestries, musical instruments, and hunting paraphernalia. The juxtaposition between these ethnographic objects and Zaurbekova’s pieces is striking, but barely addressed by a wall text relating Zaurbekova’s philosophy to that of the Swiss constructivist Sophie Taeuber-Arp. Against the classical tapestries’ palettes and designs, Zaurbekova’s experimentation with figuration and abstraction in works such as In the Yurt (1985) is perceptibly expressive and bold. Even in these early examples, her deceptively unfettered designs resemble freehand painting, and her bright, complex color combinations and transitions are underpinned by technical finesse and confidence.

BATIMA ZAURBEKOVA ’s “Threads of Heritage” at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts, Almaty, 2026. Photo by Kirill Fedorov. Courtesy the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts.

During the 1970s, Kazakhstan experienced rapid industrialization and urbanization alongside the coterminous crises of the Aral Sea’s collapse, continued Soviet nuclear testing at Semipalatinsk in the northeast, and severe environmental degradation from Khrushchev’s disastrous Virgin Lands campaign. Against such irreversible and even existential transformation, the quixotic quest for ecological, social, and cultural harmony underpins Zaurbekova’s monumental tapestries in the exhibition’s second section. Large-scale works such as Vastness (1975), Kazakhstan (1977), and Mother Earth (1984) are most remarkable for their semi-abstract compositions integrating human figures, mountains, trees, and water; wind, air, and light are invested with color, shape, and solidity. Mother Earth , which Zaurbekova highlights as perhaps her most technically demanding project, showcases the artist’s virtuoso dexterity in wave-shaped flourishes merging motifs of land, agriculture, and women. The exhibition’s centerpiece, Vastness , presents a majestic prelapsarian vision of the world, coalescing around a stylized yurt and female figure surrounded by radiant waves of musicians, flora, and fauna. Its kaleidoscopic color gradation is highly intricate and precise, depicting even tiny figures’ cheekbones with intimacy, while unifying diverse landscape elements in an overarching symphony of color. Zaurbekova estimates that this tapestry, measuring 207 by 361 centimeters, took around six months to make; she notes that the selection of thread colors was often the most demanding part of the process, particularly when depicting highly gradated planes of color.

Installation views of BATIMA ZAURBEKOVA ’s “Threads of Heritage” at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts, Almaty, 2026. Photos by Kirill Fedorov. Courtesy the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts.

Zaurbekova’s intensive period of creativity in the late 1970s and ’80s was matched by increasing professional recognition. In 1977, the state commissioned her and three fellow artists to produce a 100-square-meter tapestry for the Kazakhstan Hotel. The landmark work, Rainbow , took two years to produce and is featured in Melody , a documentary about Zaurbekova produced by Kazakhfilm in 1977. After the Soviet Union’s collapse and Kazakhstan’s independence in 1991, Zaurbekova decamped to Turkey, seeking respite from the exhaustion of these transitional years. The immediate post-Soviet period presented difficult times for Kazakhstani artists as the Ministry of Culture stopped commissioning artworks. However, expanding opportunities for interaction with other countries fostered greater cultural exchange and growing public interest in the arts. In 1997, the Soros Foundation opened the Soros Center for Contemporary Art in Almaty; despite criticisms of its harboring a neoliberal agenda, it functioned as an important platform for independent artists before closing 10 years later.

BATIMA ZAURBEKOVA ’s “Threads of Heritage” at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts, Almaty, 2026. Photo by Kirill Fedorov. Courtesy the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts.

Kazakhstan’s early years of independence find material expression in Zaurbekova’s experimentation with space, time, and motion. She created multiple oil paintings and tapestries of Almaty and Astana in the 2000s, capturing the metropolises in their most dynamic period of post-Soviet economic boom. Here, her skyscrapers pulse with muscular, radiant prisms of color, as if the buildings were literally arching sunward like blooming shoots. It is also delightful to see Zaurbekova’s reworking of certain motifs across decades; in the exhibition catalog, the curators have helpfully juxtaposed several such pairs. The progression of her Still Life canvases from 1978, 1989, 2004, and 2006 is reminiscent of visits to an old friend over many years, marked by new adventures and accumulating wrinkles, where you are always received with joie de vivre and a platter of fresh oranges. Today, Zaurbekova is one of the state’s most illustrious artists: she is an Honored Worker of Culture of the Republic of Kazakhstan and a recipient of the Order of Otan, one of Kazakhstan’s most prestigious civilian awards. Days after her 80th birthday, her exhibition opens on the cusp of a new era of Kazakhstani contemporary art, most prominently heralded by the 2025 inaugurations of the Almaty Museum of Art and the Tselinny Center of Contemporary Culture. Both projects, underwritten by Kazakhstani entrepreneurs, are part of bold visions inscribing Almaty’s star within the global circuits of contemporary art and creative capital. The muralnomads are embarking upon another brave new world.

“Threads of Heritage” is on view at Almaty’s Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts from September 25 to November 8, 2026.

Chin-chin Yap is a Singaporean writer and filmmaker based in Lisbon, and a contributing editor for ArtAsiaPacific.

article_text:
“Motherfucking Utah, let’s go!”

That was the spirit inside the energetic Oct. 22 opening night screening at FilmQuest . The 10-day festival in Provo launched its 13th installment with a screening of the Utah-made motorcycle action feature, “ Whiskey Throttle .”

Upon entering the festival’s screening home at the Velour Live Music Gallery, the audience was greeted with a comfortable auditorium with plenty of spooky decorations, an intoxicating popcorn smell and the sound of new friends being made and potential collaborators being introduced. Vintage ’80s movie trailers for films like “Masters of the Universe” and era-appropriate toy commercials rolled on the screen as people gathered, contributing to the fandom vibe.

Related Stories

Starz Beats Wall Street's Q3 Earnings Estimates as Net Loss Narrows to $35 Million, Linear TV Revenue Dips

Byron Allen Earns Profit After Selling All the Starz Stock He Bought From Steven Mnuchin

Helping to amp up the audience was FilmQuest founder and director Jonathan Martin, a one-man cheerleading squad for both Utah filmmaking and genre fare. He introduced the night playing to the crowd — throwing some friendly barbs at both Sundance for packing up and leaving the state, and at neighbor-to-the-north Idaho.

The local humor played well in the room, as did a notice during FilmQuest’s opening announcements that none of the films in the festival used AI. This brought a round of applause, unsurprising in a room filled with indie creatives who believe that AI is both threatening their jobs and lowering the quality of art.

“Whiskey Throttle” kept the hometown crowd on the edge of their seats, with frequent cheers for all of the film’s explosions, dazzling desert motorcycle camerawork and practical stunt work. Jacob Schwarz directed the story of a biker gang pursuing a mysterious rider who killed a cartel leader and stole his crypto wallet.

In the Q&A following the premiere, Dave Hunter, who produced the film under his new Utah-based Intension Industries banner, spoke to the hometown feel of the production, saying, “My entire family is involved. All of my kids were the stunt riders … We had everybody that we knew involved in this film.”

Utah Film Commission Production Manager Derek Mellus was on hand toasting the production and highlighted how the team took advantage of the state’s scenic locations for the film.

“If you have a road movie, you should be shooting it in Utah,” Mellus told Variety . “Whether it’s going to higher elevation or to the deserts or to southern Utah, Red Rocks, we have it all here.”

Prior to “Whiskey Throttle,” two short films were screened, as per the fest’s tradition of pairing thematically similar shorts with the main attraction.

“Relict” was also local, springing out of Brigham Young University’s Department of Theatre and Media Arts. Written by, directed and shot by twin brothers Andrew and James Harker, the atmospheric tale of an anthropologist obsessed with getting the perfect photograph of a mysterious creature was visually arresting, especially considering it was the duo’s senior thesis. At the end of the Q&A, Martin noted that the Harkers have a script for a feature-length version that they’d love to make.

Also playing was the funny Australian short “Marv,” a parody of the “Saw” series where the titular clown tortures a man and his family. Yet, it becomes something of a gore-filled episode of “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” as Marv realizes he made a mistake and might have to stop his traps early. Writer-director Andrew Gardner has such a keen knack for comic timing that it’d be a treat to see him helm a chapter in the “Scary Movie” franchise someday.

After the Q&A, the crowd remained buzzy and eager, but Martin had to boot the chitchatters to talk outside, given “Whiskey Throttle” had a packed late show eager to come in and keep the celebration of Utah filmmaking rolling on.

“Whiskey Throttle” is being represented for sales by Scatena & Rosner Films.

article_text:
Kehrer Verlag releases José Antonio Rosas : Somewhere We Feel Free .

For a decade, José Antonio Rosas has photographed from deep inside the crowds at some of the world’s great gatherings. From music festivals and religious pilgrimages to cultural rites, he found a common impulse: the desire to step outside everyday life and experience a sense of connection and release.

In 2015, standing in a crowd at Glastonbury Festival, José Antonio Rosas experienced a sense of collective euphoria that stayed with him. Over the next ten years, he followed this feeling across four continents, photographing seven of the world’s great gatherings—from the explosion of colour at India’s Holi, the candlelit devotion of Christmas in Lalibela, the vibrant dances of Peru’s Candelaria, the icy pilgrimage to Qoyllur Rit’i in the Andes, the vast human tide of Kumbh Mela and the unrestrained joy of Brazil’s Carnaval.

Though separated by culture, geography and purpose, these gatherings share a powerful common thread: the suspension of ordinary life and the collective release of uninhibited emotion. Within the press of bodies and the roar of music or prayer, individuality does not disappear, it transforms. Closed eyes, open mouths and gestures of serenity or ecstasy become expressions of freedom, connection and transcendence.

Somewhere We Feel Free moves across cultures, faiths and continents, revealing the shared human impulse to gather, to surrender and, somewhere within the crowd, to feel free.

With an essay by art critic Jean Dykstra and an interview with José Antonio Rosas by artist Janelle Lynch, the publication brings together this powerful decade-long body of work in the photographer’s second monograph.

José Antonio Rosas is a documentary photographer based in Lima, Peru. He has built his work through repeated visits and sustained attention to mass celebrations, religious pilgrimages, remote wildlife, and communities far from home. His award-winning work has been exhibited and published internationally.

Jean Dykstra is an arts writer and editor. The former editor of photograph magazine, she writes The Photosphere , a Substack publication about contemporary photography. She’s contributed to numerous publications, including The New York Review of Books , The Brooklyn Rail , and Dear Dave .

Janelle Lynch is an artist, writer, and educator, based in New York City. She is represented by Flowers Gallery and has three monographs published by Radius Books. Lynch teaches at the International Center of Photography and writes for LensCulture and The Brooklyn Rail .

article_text:
Joe Manganiello , who was set to reprise the role of Deathstroke in Ben Affleck’s scrapped Batman film, is telling all about what would have happened had the superhero film made it to theaters.

In his new memoir “Bloodlines,” published on Tuesday, the actor wrote that Affleck, who was attached as the writer, director, producer and star, planned to make the film “a superhero version of David Fincher’s ‘The Game’” in which Deathstroke would “dismantle Batman’s entire life” after being made to think the Caped Crusader killed his son (via EW ).

Related Stories

'Coven Academy' Renewed for Season 2 at Disney

Manganiello, who first played Deathstroke, a DC supervillain, briefly in 2017’s “Justice League,” wrote that murdering Commissioner Gordon, holding Alfred Pennyworth hostage and breaking into the Batcave would all be a part of Deathstroke’s revenge plan, and that the film would have included a fight in which “Deathstroke would nearly kill both Batman and Batgirl before they would both escape via an aboveground train.”

According to the “Magic Mike” actor, the film would have concluded with a “climactic one-on-one showdown through the streets of Gotham.” “It sounded good to me,” Manganiello wrote. “I told Ben how great I thought his films were, especially ‘The Town,’ and how I was really looking forward to seeing his Best Picture version of a Batman movie.” He went on to explain that Affleck’s roles on set sounded like “a lot” for a single person, to which the “Argo” director responded: “Yeah, I know…But don’t worry, you’re in good hands. You’re in good hands, man.”

Ultimately, the film never came out. Recently, Ben Affleck appeared on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast and called the “ Justice League ” reshoots the “low point of my career.”

“The experience of ‘Justice League’ was so negative for lots of different reasons, some of which have to do with where I was at personally and some of which had to do with the tragedy that happened at that time,” Affleck said. “I saw how not to make a movie like that, which is where the studio is at odds with the filmmaker. You are really making a mistake. I was really glad and gratified that Zack got to release [his version via the Snyder Cut]. That was fucking great. I was really happy for him. That was shitty, him being taken off that movie and the reshoots that we did. If you want the low point of my career, it was that.”

article_text:
「ART TAIPEI 2026」には台湾国内外127のギャラリーが集結

台湾を代表する国際アートフェア「ART TAIPEI 2026」が、10月30日から11月2日まで台北世界貿易センター展示ホール1で開催される。第33回となる今回のテーマは「共生（Symbiosis）」。10月24日からは、台北市内の美術館やギャラリーなどを横断する「Taipei Art Week 2026」も開催される。

1992年に創設されたART TAIPEIは、台湾画廊協会が主催するアジア有数の歴史を持つ国際アートフェア。今年は台湾から66、海外から61の計127ギャラリーが出展する。台湾からはティナ・ケン・ギャラリー（Tina Keng Gallery）、リャン・ギャラリー（Liang Gallery）、アジアアートセンター（Asia Art Center）、イ・ユン・アート（YI YUN ART）、イリ・アーツ（YIRI ARTS）などが参加。海外からはパリを拠点に世界各地に展開するペロタンや、シンガポールのリチャード・コー・ファイン・アート（Richard Koh Fine Art）などが名を連ねる。日本からは、村上隆が設立したKaikai Kiki Galleryが数年ぶりに参加する。

2008年以降の日本のアートシーンに焦点を当てた特別セクションも

今回の注目のひとつが、日本の現代アートに焦点を当てた特別セクション「Turning the Frown Upside-Down」だ。東京を拠点とするミサコアンドローゼン（MISAKO & ROSEN）のジェフリー・イアン・ローゼン（Jeffrey Ian Rosen）がキュレーションを担当。日本の主要ギャラリーやインディペンデント・アートスペース、実験的なアート団体が参加し、2008年以降の日本のアートシーンの変化を紹介する。

フェア全体のテーマである「共生（Symbiosis）」では、テクノロジーの急速な発展と現代社会の変化を背景に、人間と技術の関係性を問い直す。身体的な労働の痕跡や素材の特性に着目した作品、東洋の水墨表現と西洋の抽象表現を横断する試みなど、多様なアプローチが展開される。また、ブースを「一時的な美術館」へと転換し、従来のアートフェアの商業的な枠組みに挑戦する展示も予定されている。さらに今年は、公式ウェブサイトにAIを活用した来場者向けデジタルアシスタントを初導入。参加ギャラリーや作品の情報、会場内のおすすめルート、プログラムの案内などを多言語で提供し、来場者の鑑賞体験をサポートする。

フェアと同時期に「Taipei Art Week 2026」も開催

フェアに先立ち、10月24日には「速度（Velocity）」をテーマに掲げる「Taipei Art Week 2026」が開幕する。台北市内の80以上のギャラリー、美術館、アート機関が連携し、展覧会や特別プログラムを展開する。

10月27日には台北市立美術館で国際フォーラム「Curating Now: Responding to the Present」を開催。2025年ジョグジャ・ビエンナーレのキュレーターを務めたエヴァ・リン（Eva Lin）をモデレーターに、香港のM+でキュラトリアル部門を率いるラッセル・ストーラー（Russell Storer）、2026年ヴェネチア・ビエンナーレ韓国館のキュレーターを務めるビンナ・チェ（Binna Choi）が登壇し、現代アートをめぐる国際的なネットワークやキュレーションのあり方を議論する。

アートフェアの枠を超えて都市全体に広がるプログラムを通じて、台湾と国際的なアートシーンの現在地を紹介する機会となりそうだ。

開催概要

ART TAIPEI 2026

会期：10月30日〜11月2日（VIPプレビュー：10月29日、30日）

会場：台北世界貿易センター展示ホール1

公式ホームページ： https://2026.art-taipei.com/

Taipei Art Week 2026

会期：2026年10月24日〜11月2日

会場：台北市内の参加美術館、ギャラリー、アート機関など

公式ホームページ： https://taipeiartweek.tw/

article_text:
More than a decade after she was first diagnosed, Dame Judi Dench ‘s vision loss has taken her off the stage and screen.

The Oscar winner recently revealed that she “can’t do a play anymore” and “can’t do a film anymore” following her diagnosis with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in 2012.

“I can’t be on stage,” said Dench on BBC Radio 4’s Today . “I can’t do a play anymore. I can’t do a film anymore. I can’t read anymore.”

Related Stories

Judi Dench Details Worsening Eyesight Due To Macular Degeneration: “I Can’t See Anymore”

London’s Shaftesbury Theatre To Be Renamed The Judi Dench Theatre

Dench noted that her vision loss has resulted in some awkward moments, as she has approached to wrong person “and give them an almost hug” on multiple occasions.

Watch on Deadline

While Dench is effectively retired from the stage and screen, she still plans to make public appearances and speak about her condition, noting “the radio has always been important to me.”

Having first revealed her AMD diagnosis in 2012, which is a disease that blurs a person’s central vision by causing damage to the macula, Dench has discussed her potential retirement in recent years.

Dench most recently voiced a smart fridge invented by Claire Foy’s Polly in The Magic Faraway Tree , which premiered earlier this year, based on Enid Blyton’s book series. Her last onscreen appearances include roles in Belfast (2021) and Allelujah (2022), as well as a cameo in Spirited (2022).

article_text:
フォトグラファーMARCOによる個展「still blue」が、2026年10月7日（水）から25日（日）まで、東京・代官山のSPEAK FOR WALLで開催される。MARCOにとって約5年ぶりとなる都内での個展で、ライフワークとして制作を続けてきた水中写真シリーズの新たな展開を披露する。

ファッション写真やアーティストのポートレートなどを数多く手がけ、独特の色彩感覚とアイデア、軽やかなフットワークで知られるMARCO。ファインダー越しに人物を風景として捉える一方、その背後にある物語だけでなく、裏側に潜む社会的な情報にも眼差しを向けてきた。一方、2016年頃からは水中写真によるオリジナル作品を発表。旅先で海に潜り、波に舞い上がる砂やきらめく光彩などを捉えながら、海中で見つけた宇宙を表現してきた。2021年の写真集『lost in the blue』では、あえて色を排除することで海中世界をモノクロームで描き出している。

「still blue」では、そうした水中写真の現在地を提示。モノクロのシリーズに加え、透明フィルムを用いたコラージュ作品約7点を発表する。さらに、水中の風景写真を居住空間に調和させる試みとして、軸装作品も都内では初めて展示・販売。写真作品と掛け軸のサイズや生地を組み合わせ、会場でセミオーダーすることもできるという。

MARCOは長野県生まれ。慶應義塾大学在学中から蜷川実花に師事し、2008年よりフリーランスのフォトグラファーとして活動。エディトリアルや広告、ポートレート撮影のほか、個展やウェブなどで作品を発表している。写真集に『PARCO de MARCO』『lost in the blue』『SOMEWHERE NOWHERE』など。

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "曾经由色情片涉足的领域，如今恐怖片已成为渗透并模仿所有其他类型的流派。随着近期大量版权过期的卡通角色被掘墓翻新成不太新鲜的IP，现在古典文学显然也成了血腥华丽升级的目标，在这个案例中，则是艾米莉·勃朗特那本常令中考学生头疼的名著。但贝卡·希拉尼（Becca Hirani）吃力不讨好的重构，让原著中的哥特式潜台词变得生硬直接、鲜血四溅。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如小说中一样，睁大眼睛的洛克伍德先生（罗斯·汤森-格林饰）在呼啸山庄对阴郁的地主希斯克利夫（斯カイ·奇马饰）进行了礼节性拜访。但这一次，他的逗留更像是乔纳森·哈克在德古拉城堡的经历；无论他转向何处，希斯克利夫挚爱的凯瑟琳·欧肖（艾尔·奥哈拉饰）那披着面纱的幽灵都在潜伏，她在著名的夜间显现时，在窗台上留下了额外的一滩血迹。这位脾气暴躁的主人并没有让洛克伍德感到安心——甚至在他被一种引发腹股沟淋巴结炎的疾病困扰并困在房子里之前。在幻觉、乖戾的仆人，以及希斯克利夫传闻中的儿子林顿的诡异缺席之间，他开始惊恐地意识到自己误入了一种完全不同的沼泽地故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "希拉尼付出了不可否认的努力，使她的情节设定与勃朗特的保持一致——尽管大多数角色（包括可怜的老洛克伍德的马）都迎来了更为残酷的命运。通过凯瑟琳日记的片段、管家内莉（尼科拉·赖特饰）的吐露，以及更多涉及洛克伍德的随机超自然闪回，庄园的前史被讲述得有些杂乱无章，尽管其中带有希斯克利夫作为18世纪约克郡开膛手这种夸张的噱头。不同于凯特·布什和埃默拉尔德·芬内尔在各自改编作品中那样放大坎普风，希拉尼的处理严肃而阴沉，而且考虑到她塞进去了额外的勒死、砍杀和草叉穿刺，这种严肃令人感到莫名其妙。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与此同时，怯懦的演技削弱了这部电影作为纯粹砍杀片的说服力：汤森-格林神经质的表演让人觉得他仿佛是从《万事皆休》中误入此地，而尽管有着拉斯普京般的外表，声音飘忽的奇马却显得过于松散，难以让人相信他是一个拜伦式的坏男孩。在大部分片长中，我们几乎看不到什么能让人信服他转变为杀人狂魔的动机，直到最后一分钟才揭晓他针对其受监护人凯茜（安娜·库佩饰）的、类似《养鬼吃人》的阴谋。以这种摇摇欲坠的方式重唤勃朗特的尸体，这次翻新不仅显得毫无意义，而且缺乏自我认知或趣味。", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "电影", "links": [{"text": "Film", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/film"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "恐怖片", "links": [{"text": "Horror films", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/horror"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "艾米莉·勃朗特", "links": [{"text": "Emily Brontë", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/books/emilybronte"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "影评", "links": [{"text": "reviews", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tone/reviews"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
W here pornography once trod, horror has now become the genre that infiltrates and apes all others. With a host of out-of-copyright cartoon characters recently grave-robbed for not-so-fresh IP, now classic literature is apparently fair game for a gruesome glow-up, in this case, Emily Brontë’s regular GCSE-botherer. But Becca Hirani’s laboured reworking makes the book’s gothic subtext crashingly, jugular-spurtingly textual.

As in the novel, wide-eyed Mr Lockwood (Ross Townsend-Green) pays a courtesy call to his brooding landlord Heathcliff (Sky Cheema) at Wuthering Heights. But this time, his sojourn is more like Jonathan Harker’s at Dracula’s castle; everywhere he turns, the shrouded phantom of Heathcliff’s beloved Catherine Earnshaw (Elle O’Hara) is lurking, and she leaves an extra dollop of gore on the windowsill in her famous nocturnal apparition. The tetchy host doesn’t do much to put Lockwood at ease – even before he’s trapped in the house by a bubo-inflicting malady. Between the hallucinations, the surly servants, and the weird absence of Heathcliff’s rumoured son Linton, he begins freaking out that it’s a different kind of moors story he’s stumbled into.

Hirani puts undeniable effort in getting her plot points to line up with Brontë’s – even if most of the characters, including poor old Lockwood’s horse, meet a much grislier fate. Rationed out in snippets of Catherine’s diary, the confidences of housekeeper Nelly (Nicola Wright) and more random supernatural flashbacks involving Lockwood, the manor’s backstory is rather garbled, though with the OTT hook of Heathcliff as an 18th-century Yorkshire Ripper. Rather than amping up the camp, as the likes of Kate Bush and Emerald Fennell did in their takes on the novel, Hirani plays it straight and dour, mystifyingly so, given the extra stranglings, slashings and pitchfork-impalings she’s chucked in.

At the same time, diffident acting undermines the film’s claim as pure slasher fare: Townsend-Green’s jumpy turn feels as if he has strayed out of Jeeves and Wooster, while, despite the Rasputin looks, windy-voiced Cheema is too loose to convince as Byronic bad boy. For much of the runtime, we’re left with too little that makes his conversion to homicidal mania credible, until the last-minute lowdown on his Hellraiser-like scheme for his ward, Cathy (Anna Coupé). Reanimating the corpse of Brontë in this rickety way, this update not only feels pointless, but short on self-awareness or fun.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为名为“Collected”的展览的一部分，巴勃罗·毕加索、勒内·马格里特、卢西安·弗洛伊德和约翰·康斯太布尔的艺术作品将于明年在伦敦国家美术馆汇聚一堂。", "links": [{"text": "René Magritte", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/gagosian-rene-magritte-exhibition-london-frieze-2026-1234793166/"}, {"text": "National Gallery in London", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/national-gallery-in-london/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些作品通过两个项目获得：由英格兰艺术委员会代表英国政府组织的“以物抵税”（Acceptance in Lieu）和“文化礼品”（Cultural Gifts）计划。前者是一项允许通过将重要或杰出的文化、科学或历史藏品移交给国家来抵消遗产税账单的倡议，而“文化礼品”计划则允许英国纳税人通过交换重要物件来减少捐赠者的企业所得税、个人所得税或资本利得税负。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Collected”将于5月22日开幕并一直持续到9月5日，随后将巡展至苏格兰国家美术馆、北爱尔兰阿尔斯特博物馆以及威尔士国家博物馆（Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales）。展览将展出40件作品，从毕加索的《哭泣的女人》（1937）、弗洛伊德的《赫敏·斯科特肖像》（1960）到圭尔奇诺的《萨摩斯西比拉与一个小爱神》（1651）。毕加索的两件陶瓷作品也将一同展出：《巢中鸟》（1949）和《花卉女性/站立的裸体》（1948），此外还有中国瓷器花盆。", "links": [{"text": "Chinese porcelain", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/chinese-imperial-porcelain-christies-marchant-market-1234679557/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/NG6613-A5c.jpg?w=400", "alt": "老安布罗斯·博斯查特，《万历花瓶台架上的静物：繁花、贝壳与蝴蝶》，1609-10年。", "caption": "老安布罗斯·博斯查特，《万历花瓶台架上的静物：繁花、贝壳与蝴蝶》，1609-10年。国家美术馆", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "国家美术馆馆长加布里埃尔·玛丽亚·菲纳尔迪爵士（Sir Gabriele Maria Finaldi）在一份声明中表示，“怎么高估‘以物抵税’和‘文化礼品’计划在将令人惊叹的艺术品纳入英国各地博物馆公共所有权方面的重要性都不为过。国家美术馆非常高兴能与横跨四个国家的合作伙伴共同庆祝这一文化盛宴。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该收藏中其他令人瞩目的艺术品包括归属于伦勃朗的《扶手椅中的老人》（1650）；保罗·塞尚的《尚蒂伊林荫大道》（1888）；彼得·多伊格的《小镇边缘》（1986-88）；以及来自诺福克博物馆服务的马格里特的《人类的状况》（1935）。随着高古轩画廊举办展期至12月12日的展览“这依然不是烟斗：马格里特的后世”，马格里特一直以来都是伦敦的热门话题。", "links": [{"text": "Rembrandt", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/rembrandt/"}, {"text": "Magritte", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/magritte/"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
Artworks by Pablo Picasso, René Magritte , Lucian Freud, and John Constable are coming together next year at the National Gallery in London , as part of an exhibition titled “Collected.”

The works have been acquired through two programs: the Acceptance in Lieu and Cultural Gifts schemes, organized by the Arts Council England on behalf of the UK government. The first is an initiative that allows an inheritance tax bill to be replaced by transferring important or pre-eminent cultural, scientific, or historic allocations to the nation, while the Cultural Gifts scheme lets UK taxpayers swap objects of importance in return for a reduction in the donor’s corporation, income, or capital gains tax liability.

“Collected” will open on May 22 and run through to September 5, and will then travel to the National Galleries of Scotland, the Ulster Museum in Northern Ireland, and the Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales. The show will feature 40 works, from Picasso’s The Weeping Woman (1937) and Freud’s Portrait of Hermione Scott (1960) to Guercino’s The Samian Sibyl with a Putto (1651). Two ceramics by Picasso will also be displayed: Bird on a Nest (1949) and Flower Women/Standing Nudes (1948), alongside Chinese porcelain jardiniere.

Sir Gabriele Maria Finaldi, director of the National Gallery, said in a statement that it’s “impossible to overestimate the importance of the Acceptance in Lieu and Cultural Gift Scheme in bringing astounding works of art into public ownership in museums across the UK. The National Gallery is delighted to celebrate this cultural cornucopia with our partners across the four nations.”

Other impressive artworks in the collection include An Old Man in an Armchair (1650) that is attributed to Rembrandt ; Paul Cézanne’s Avenue at Chantilly (1888); Peter Doig’s At the Edge of Town (1986-88); and Magritte ’s La condition humaine (1935), from the Norfolk Museums Service. Magritte has been the talk of London with Gagosian Gallery’s show “This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte” on view until December 12.

article_text:
Quentin Tarantino surprised the crowd during a Q&A and screening of his 10-time Oscar-nominated Once Upon a Time in Hollywood on Friday night at AFI Fest in Los Angeles by screening the first 17 minutes of its sequel The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth .

It marks the first public look at the film, a follow-up to Hollywood that Tarantino scripted and David Fincher directed. Brad Pitt revises his Oscar-winning role as Booth, a stuntman and sidekick to Leonardo DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton in the original 2019 film.

Related Stories

‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: Brad Pitt Revisits The Character That Won Him An Oscar In David Fincher’s Latest

‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’: New Photos Of Film Starring Brad Pitt, Elizabeth Debicki, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II & More

Netflix is gearing up for the Cliff Booth theatrical release November 25 in Imax before hitting the streamer beginning December 23.

Watch on Deadline

“Well, I could talk a little bit about The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , or I could show you the first 17 minutes,” Tarantino said at the end of his special-event Q&A session at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood. He had just been asked about the film and how it came about, and if he had anything else to say before the conversation wrapped.

He then stood up as the crowd began to figure out what was coming.

Here’s the moment:

Quentin Tarantino reflects on the decision to revisit Cliff Booth as he introduces the first 17 minutes of ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ at AFI Fest pic.twitter.com/0flrYw0J73 — Deadline (@DEADLINE) October 24, 2026

Cliff Booth fast-forwards to 1977 from the original film’s 1969 timeline. The new logline: Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s great and, sometimes, not so good.

The pic also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Peter Weller, Matt Groove, JB Tadena, Corey Fogelmanis and Karren Karagulian.

Buzz for the film has been building since it was announced in 2024 that Pitt and Fincher were teaming on the project that Tarantino originally wanted to direct. Fincher said earlier this week that he had to cut 60 pages from Tarantino’s script, after he said the first draft he read was 230 pages. “It was essentially two movies,” Fincher told Empire .

The final cut of the film, Fincher said, has a runtime of around 2 1/2 hours.

During tonight’s AFI Fest event, Tarantino also talked about his upcoming play The Popinjay Cavalier , which will premiere in London’s West End next spring. Sacha Baron Cohen will star in the director’s first stage play, which begins previews February 23 and opens March 18 at the Phoenix Theatre.

Quentin Tarantino on his debut stage play, which stars Sacha Baron Cohen and will open on the West End next year pic.twitter.com/jMUAJpEuCN — Deadline (@DEADLINE) October 24, 2026

Patrick Hipes contributed to this report.

article_text:
Artículos

Bad Boys 3… ¿sin Michael Bay pero con Will Smith?

Julio Vélez

Jerry Bruckheimer, Will Smith y Martin Lawrence podrían regresar para la segunda secuela de Policías rebeldes. ¿Pesará la ausencia de Michael Bay?

Deadline reveló que Sony Pictures tiene intenciones de revivir la franquicia policíaca de Dos policías rebeldes , anteriormente dirigida por Michael Bay, con la nueva entrega Bad Boys 3. Para esta, se habla sobre el posible regreso de Will Smith y Martin Lawrence como protagonistas.

Los estudios ya se encuentran en charlas con David Guggenheim ( Protegiendo al enemigo , 2012) para que escriba la historia. Sin embargo, lo que más llama la atención es que parece que el director Michael Bay , quien dirigió las primeras dos películas de la saga en 1995 y 2003, no está vinculado de forma alguna con este proyecto.

Quien sí regresa como productor, una vez concluida su relación con Disney , es Jerry Bruckheimer , aunque intriga saber cómo lo hará ya que recientemente firmó un contrato con Paramount .

¿Qué opinan? ¿Creen que sea buena idea traer de vuelta a estos personajes? Más de $100 millones de dólares en ganancias con la secuela en 2003 parecen ser una buena razón para Sony.

Julio Vélez Colaborador en web y revista Cine PREMIERE desde 2006. Me especializo en anime/manga, comics, doblaje, tecnología y videojuegos. Mis sagas favoritas: Doctor Who, Star Trek, Dragon Ball y Star Wars. Batimaníaco, geek ochentero y hardcore gamer.

title_original: Dealer Adam Shopkorn’s Alternative Route to Frieze London With Haitian Artist Myrlande Constant
editorial_title_zh: 艺术品商亚当·肖普科恩携手海地艺术家米尔朗德·孔斯坦开启通往伦敦弗里兹艺博会的另类之路
editorial_excerpt_zh: 随着来自机构和收藏家对其代理艺术家的需求飙升，这家Fort Gansevoort画廊的经营者正闯入虎穴。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "总部位于纽约的Fort Gansevoort画廊的艺术品商亚当·肖普科恩（Adam Shopkorn）在处理他于2015年与妻子卡罗琳·泰特·安杰尔（Carolyn Tate Angel）共同创立的画廊业务时，一直采取非正统的路线。在今年2月参加洛杉矶弗里兹艺博会之后，他将于本周携一场聚焦海地艺术家米尔朗德·孔斯坦（Myrlande Constant）纺织旗帜作品的个人展位亮相该艺博会的伦敦版，目前这位艺术家在她的祖国正处于紧急状态中。", "links": [{"text": "Frieze", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/frieze/"}, {"text": "Myrlande Constant", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/myrlande-constant-fort-gansevoort-representation-1234611268/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "伦敦弗里兹艺博会将标志着他今年参加的第三个艺博会，此前他上一次参展是在2020年1月。“现在对我们来说，身处这些地方很重要，”肖普科恩在前往伦敦前通过Zoom通话告诉ARTnews，并指出在2022年威尼斯双年展、2024年第6届Prospect以及2025年圣保罗双年展上亮相之后，过去几年间对孔斯坦作品的需求急剧飙升。", "links": [{"text": "Frieze London", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/frieze-london/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在伦敦弗里兹艺博会上，他将展出孔斯坦的五件巨型纺织品，定价在90,000美元至450,000美元之间。每件作品都从扎根于非洲之根的海地伏都教（Vodou）精神实践中汲取灵感。例如，尺寸超过10英尺乘9英尺的《Amwan Agwe…》（2026年），描绘了青山碧波，以及向纪念海地亡灵的年度节日Fèt Gede致敬的骷髅、蜡烛和鱼。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MC288_HR.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "米尔朗德·孔斯坦，《Amwan Agwe…》，2026年。图片由艺术家与纽约Fort Gansevoort画廊提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些最新的作品也反映了孔斯坦自身工作方式的改变，因为她已经无法像过去那样在太子港维持一间工作室了。因为她过去曾与一个女性团队合作制作她所广为人知的精美细节作品。现在，她在奔波之中制作她那些工艺复杂的装饰旗帜。由于海地持续不断的暴力冲突，为了安全起见，她不得不频繁穿梭于不同的城市之间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "自2023年底以来，肖普科恩可能会长达数月听不到孔斯坦的消息，无论是想知道她是否平安，还是她的下一批作品进展如何。但随后，在某一天突如其来的时刻，他会在纽约收到一件她超乎寻常大小的作品，这件作品经由多米尼加共和国从海地运达。“没有那种专门去太子港收集艺术品以参加伦敦艺博会的白手套精细艺术服务卡车，”肖普科恩说，并指出她的作品确实及时运达，得以在伦敦展出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MC281_HR.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "米尔朗德·孔斯坦，《Lasirène Diamant》，2025年。图片由艺术家与纽约Fort Gansevoort画廊提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了支持孔斯坦的创作，肖普科恩采取了一种更为传统老派的合作模式，以生活津贴的形式向她汇款，而不是等待销售完成并像如今的常态那样进行50-50的分成。“如果我们那样做，她就要等上无限长的时间了，”他说，并补充说，为了适应这种结构，收益往往会被“以许多不同的方式切分”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管孔斯坦可能无法稳定地使用互联网和电话服务与肖普科恩交流，但要了解她想表达的内容，最好的去处就是她的纺织品。《Lasirène Diamant》（2025年）描绘了统治海洋的女性伏都教神灵Lasirène，画面的一侧展现了这位头戴象征繁荣的钻石项链的美人鱼神灵，而另一侧则展现她坐在一艘装满水果、蛋糕和糖果的木筏上，周围环绕着美人鱼、海豚、海马和章鱼等海洋生物。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“米尔朗德正在海地艰难求生并照顾她的家人，”肖普科恩说。“一件艺术品一离开她的手，她就对之后发生的事情不太感兴趣了。当她的某件作品进入永久收藏时，这对她来说并不重要，因为她满脑子担心的都是家人的安全。”", "translated": true}]

After participating at Frieze Los Angeles this past February, he will show at the fair’s London edition this week with a solo booth dedicated to the textile flags of Haitian artist Myrlande Constant , who is living in a state of emergency in her home country.", "links": [{"text": "Frieze", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/frieze/"}, {"text": "Myrlande Constant", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/myrlande-constant-fort-gansevoort-representation-1234611268/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Frieze London will mark his third fair this year after last showing at one in January 2020. “It’s important for us to be in these places now,” Shopkorn told ARTnews on a Zoom call before heading to London, noting that demand for Constant’s work has soared in the past few years after appearances in the 2022 Venice Biennale, Prospect.6 in 2024, and the 2025 São Paulo Bienal.", "links": [{"text": "Frieze London", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/frieze-london/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At Frieze London, he will show five of Constant’s monumental textiles, priced between $90,000 and $450,000. Each work takes its cues from Vodou spiritual practices in Haiti that are grounded in their African roots. Measuring more than 10 feet by 9 feet, Amwan Agwe… (2026), for example, depicts green hills and blue waves alongside the skulls, candles, and fish that nod to Fèt Gede, Haiti’s annual festival honoring the spirits of the dead."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MC288_HR.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Myrlande Constant, Amwan Agwe… , 2026. Courtesy the artist and Fort Gansevoort, New York", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These latest works also reflect a change in Constant’s own way of working, as she is no longer able to maintain an atelier as she once did in Port-au-Prince. For she used to worked with a team of women to produce the beautiful detailed work she has become known for. Now, she crafts her elaborately decorated flags on the go. Because of the ongoing violence in Haiti, she has to move between different cities for safety."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Since late 2023, Shopkorn might go months without hearing from Constant, whether it is to know if she is okay or how her next body of work is coming along. But then, out of the blue one day, he will receive one of her larger-than-life-size pieces in New York, arriving from Haiti via the Dominican Republic. “There’s no white-glove fine-art service truck that’s going into Port-au-Prince to collect artwork for an art fair in London,” Shopkorn said, noting that her works did arrive in time in order to go on view in London."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MC281_HR.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Myrlande Constant, Lasirène Diamant , 2025. Courtesy the artist and Fort Gansevoort, New York", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To support Constant’s production, Shopkorn approaches their relationship in a more old-school model, sending her money as a stipend instead of waiting for a sale to go through and split it 50-50 as is now the norm. “If we did that, she would be waiting forever,” he said, adding that the proceeds are often “sliced and diced in many different ways” to accommodate this structure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Though Constant may not have reliable access to internet and phone services to communicate with Shopkorn, the best place to find what she has to say is in her textiles. Lasirène Diamant (2025), depicting the feminine Vodou spirit Lasirène who rules the sea, shows the mermaid spirit wearing a diamond necklace that symbolizes prosperity on one side, while on the other, she is shown in a raft filled with fruit, cake, and sweets surrounded by creatures from the sea such as mermaids, dolphins, a seahorse, and an octopus."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Myrlande is [trying to] survive in Haiti and take care of her family,” said Shopkorn. “The moment an artwork leaves her hands, she’s not terribly interested in what happens after that. When one of her pieces enters a permanent collection, it’s not relevant to her because she’s worried about the safety of her family.”"}]

Dealer Adam Shopkorn of New York–based gallery Fort Gansevoort has always taken an unorthodox route when it comes to the business he cofounded in 2015 with his wife, Carolyn Tate Angel. After participating at Frieze Los Angeles this past February, he will show at the fair’s London edition this week with a solo booth dedicated to the textile flags of Haitian artist Myrlande Constant , who is living in a state of emergency in her home country.

Frieze London will mark his third fair this year after last showing at one in January 2020. “It’s important for us to be in these places now,” Shopkorn told ARTnews on a Zoom call before heading to London, noting that demand for Constant’s work has soared in the past few years after appearances in the 2022 Venice Biennale, Prospect.6 in 2024, and the 2025 São Paulo Bienal.

At Frieze London, he will show five of Constant’s monumental textiles, priced between $90,000 and $450,000. Each work takes its cues from Vodou spiritual practices in Haiti that are grounded in their African roots. Measuring more than 10 feet by 9 feet, Amwan Agwe… (2026), for example, depicts green hills and blue waves alongside the skulls, candles, and fish that nod to Fèt Gede, Haiti’s annual festival honoring the spirits of the dead.

These latest works also reflect a change in Constant’s own way of working, as she is no longer able to maintain an atelier as she once did in Port-au-Prince. For she used to worked with a team of women to produce the beautiful detailed work she has become known for. Now, she crafts her elaborately decorated flags on the go. Because of the ongoing violence in Haiti, she has to move between different cities for safety.

Since late 2023, Shopkorn might go months without hearing from Constant, whether it is to know if she is okay or how her next body of work is coming along. But then, out of the blue one day, he will receive one of her larger-than-life-size pieces in New York, arriving from Haiti via the Dominican Republic. “There’s no white-glove fine-art service truck that’s going into Port-au-Prince to collect artwork for an art fair in London,” Shopkorn said, noting that her works did arrive in time in order to go on view in London.

To support Constant’s production, Shopkorn approaches their relationship in a more old-school model, sending her money as a stipend instead of waiting for a sale to go through and split it 50-50 as is now the norm. “If we did that, she would be waiting forever,” he said, adding that the proceeds are often “sliced and diced in many different ways” to accommodate this structure.

Though Constant may not have reliable access to internet and phone services to communicate with Shopkorn, the best place to find what she has to say is in her textiles. Lasirène Diamant (2025), depicting the feminine Vodou spirit Lasirène who rules the sea, shows the mermaid spirit wearing a diamond necklace that symbolizes prosperity on one side, while on the other, she is shown in a raft filled with fruit, cake, and sweets surrounded by creatures from the sea such as mermaids, dolphins, a seahorse, and an octopus.

“Myrlande is [trying to] survive in Haiti and take care of her family,” said Shopkorn. “The moment an artwork leaves her hands, she’s not terribly interested in what happens after that. When one of her pieces enters a permanent collection, it’s not relevant to her because she’s worried about the safety of her family.”

article_text:
ファッションデザイナー・中里唯馬による写真展「INFERNO（インフェルノ）」が、2026年11月29日（日）まで、東京・新宿の北村写真機店で開催されている。自身がライカで撮影した自然の風景と、そこから生まれたオートクチュール作品を、写真・映像・音楽を通して紹介する。

2016年からパリ・オートクチュール・ウィークでコレクションを発表し続けている中里。自然界から着想を得て独創的な衣服を生み出す一方、自ら世界各地を訪れ、ライカで自然の姿を撮影してきた。

本展では、デジタルとフィルム、モノクロームとカラーによる作品を展示。自然から受け取ったイメージを衣服へと昇華し、その衣服を再び自然の中で写真に収めるという、中里独自の創作の循環を浮かび上がらせる。

展覧会タイトルの「INFERNO」は、カナリア諸島で目にした、月明かりの下で黒い炎のように見えた波の光景に由来する。モノクロームの風景に潜む色彩と、そこから生み出される鮮やかなファッション。異なる表現が交差する中里の世界観を提示する。

会場では、5mを超える壁面いっぱいに写真作品を展示するほか、パリ・オートクチュール・ウィークで発表されたショーの映像を音楽とともに上映。写真とファッション、映像、音楽が融合する没入型の展示空間を構成する。

また、会期中には映画プロデューサーの石井朋彦、映像作家の関根光才らを迎えたトークイベントを開催。11月27日（金）には、中里の創作活動を追ったドキュメンタリー映画『燃えるドレスを紡いで』の上映会も行われる。

editorial_title_zh: 《假面之城》影评——西区剧院鬼故事，女性版“歌剧魅影”只为复仇而来
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在一家西区剧院里，一名年轻演员听到一个虚无缥缈的声音在指导他唱歌。这是一场令人别扭的人鬼恋的开端。这部以西区剧院为背景的鬼故事比舞台上的老旧木地板还要吱呀作响。这是对《歌剧魅影》性别反转的演绎……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部以西区剧院为背景的鬼故事比舞台上的老旧木地板还要吱呀作响。这是一个带有女性幽灵的《歌剧魅影》性别反转版：极具才华的作曲家伊芙（阿曼达·江饰）在一次剧院火灾中悲惨丧生。事实果真如此吗？对于在伊芙的热门音乐剧《假面之城》复排中被选为主演的真诚年轻演员克里斯蒂安（查理·戈达德饰）而言，这就是他面临的问题。这部剧正是在她丧生的同一家剧院上演。随后，克里斯蒂安开始听到一个虚无缥缈的幽灵声音在指导他唱歌。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部电影的问题之一在于表演风格的冲突。江饰演的伊芙性感而神秘，仿佛走出了大卫·林ynch的电影。与此同时，演员迪诺·布加蒂·米奇森（Deano Bugatti Mitchison）则以《疤面煞星》中阿尔·帕西诺级别的强度来诠释复排导演——吸毒过头的剧院大亨维克托——这恐怕是西区唯一一个在办公桌抽屉里藏着上膛手枪的导演。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "维克托被怀疑卷入了那场杀死伊芙的大火，小报记者们也闻风而动。与此同时，伊芙一心只想要复仇：灯光闪烁，墙上的吊具部件纷纷脱落。不管她是不是幽灵，克里斯蒂安似乎对她产生了强烈的感情——正如任何带有幽灵与人类恋爱可能性的电影一样，这变得有点令人作呕。随着剧情的发展，这部电影变得越来越令人费解，混乱到我不得不回去又看了一遍，确信自己漏掉了什么能让剧情合情合理的关键内容。然而并没有。", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "电影", "links": [{"text": "Film", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/film"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "剧情片", "links": [{"text": "Drama films", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/drama"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "恐怖片", "links": [{"text": "Horror films", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/horror"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "音乐片", "links": [{"text": "Musicals", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/stage/musicals"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "戏剧", "links": [{"text": "Theatre", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/stage/theatre"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "惊悚片", "links": [{"text": "Thrillers", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/thriller"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "爱情片", "links": [{"text": "Romance films", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/romance"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "影评", "links": [{"text": "reviews", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tone/reviews"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
T his ghost story set in a West End theatre is creakier than the old wooden floorboards on stage. It’s a gender reversal of Phantom of the Opera with a female phantom: wildly talented composer Eve (Amanda Jiang), who died tragically in a theatre fire. Or did she? That’s the question for earnest young actor Christian (Charlie Goddard) cast as the lead in a revival of Eve’s hit musical, City of Masks. It’s being staged in the very theatre where she died. Then Christian starts hearing a ghostly disembodied voice coaching his singing.

Part of the problem with the film is a clash of acting styles. Jiang seems to have stepped out of a David Lynch film to play Eve; sensual and mysterious. Meanwhile, actor Deano Bugatti Mitchison channels Al Pacino in Scarface levels of intensity to play the revival’s director, coked-up theatre impresario Victor – surely the only director in the West End to keep a loaded gun in his desk drawer

Victor is suspected of involvement in the fire that killed Eve and the tabloids are sniffing around. Meanwhile, Eve is all out for revenge: lights flicker, bits of rigging fly off the walls. Whether or not she is a ghost, Christian seems to be developing big feelings for her – and as in any film with the prospect of ghost-on-human romance, it gets a bit ick. And as it goes on the film gets more and more baffling, so confusing that I went back and watched it again, convinced I’d missed something vital that would make sense of it. But no.
